description: Hi everyone! We are a team of two passionate students interested in space exploration, technology, and creative problem-solving. We are excited to participate in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 and turn interesting ideas into meaningful projects. We are looking for enthusiastic teammates who are interested in web development, UI/UX design, research, storytelling, or data analysis.
summary: SpaceMuse is a free, interactive online museum of twelve NASA machines left behind on the Moon and Mars, from Apollo 11's still-working laser mirror to the Ingenuity helicopter. Visitors don't browse a list: they launch on an SLS rocket, land on the Moon, track each machine down on the ground, then fly on to Mars and do the same. At every stop a museum label answers the questions a newcomer actually asks — What is it? Why is it still here? What did it teach us? What is left today? — with real NASA "then" photos and orbital "now" images. The tour opens with a question ("Are these machines junk, or history?") and ends with the answer: they are the first historic sites beyond Earth, now protected by NASA guidance (2011) and U.S. law (2020). It answers "Abandoned but not Forgotten" by turning discarded hardware into stories students can follow, hear and remember — with every fact sourced.
details:
What it does SpaceMuse is a free, interactive 3D museum of twelve NASA machines that were left behind on the Moon and Mars — from Apollo 11's laser reflector, still used today, to the Ingenuity helicopter. Instead of browsing a list, visitors go on an expedition: they launch on an SLS rocket from Launch Complex 39B, see five targets glowing on the Moon at their real coordinates, land, and track each machine down on the ground; then they fly on to Mars, enter the atmosphere, and find seven more. The journey ends in a "Hall of Silence" (the last time each machine talked to Earth) and a closing message.

How it works At every stop, a museum label answers the questions a newcomer actually asks: What is it? Why is it still here? What did it teach us? What is left today? A full panel adds the story, key dates and numbers (each with its source), sourced landing coordinates, and a Then/Now slider comparing a NASA surface photo with an orbital image of the same spot today (LRO or HiRISE). An audio tour speaks at every stop and each exhibit has its own audio guide. A tracker with a mini-map lets visitors fly to any site, and a Field Log stamps each machine they find. A 14-second GRAIL simulation paints NASA's real lunar gravity map onto the Moon.

Benefits and intended impact Students meet space history the way they meet places: by going there. A discarded machine becomes a story with a reason (why it stayed), a result (what it taught us) and a present (what is there now). The tour opens with a question — "Are these machines junk, or history?" — and answers it with NASA's 2011 guidance and the 2020 U.S. law protecting Apollo sites: these are the first historic sites beyond Earth. Our goal is a one-click classroom visit that any teacher can use, on a laptop or a phone.

How it is creative We turned a catalogue into a mission: the visitor earns each discovery by flying, landing and searching, so the 3D is not decoration but the way the story is told. The GRAIL exhibit is not a model on a shelf but a short simulation using the mission's own gravity data. Each machine ends with "what it taught us", so debris becomes discovery.

Factors our team considered

  • Accuracy: every number and date has a cited NASA or partner source; where sources disagree we do not state a number. The voyage is clearly labelled imagined, and 3D scenes are labelled illustrative reconstructions.
  • Audience: written for students with no prior knowledge — plain language, a mission briefing, and voice narration for visitors who prefer to listen.
  • Accessibility and devices: keyboard navigation, reduced-motion support, a Lightweight no-3D mode, and quality tiers so it runs on phones.
  • Honesty about AI: real NASA photos are shown unmodified and credited; AI-assisted 3D is watermarked; AI narration is disclosed in text and file metadata.
  • Respect for heritage: our generated 3D contains no NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers.

Tools TypeScript, React 19, Next.js 16, Three.js / React Three Fiber, GSAP and Lenis for scroll animation, Tailwind CSS, Vercel hosting; Playwright for automated visual and performance tests; ffmpeg for media; ElevenLabs for the exhibit narration voice; AI assistants (Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini) for research cross-checking, writing support, code and procedural 3D. Data: NASA NSSDCA, LRO/LROC, HiRISE, NASA SVS (GRAIL gravity map, CGI Moon Kit), NASA 3D Resources, NASA Image and Video Library, NASA History Program Office.
